newsitem.title: GERMANY: Eurobourses part ways with U.S., Germany best bet.
newsitem.headline: Eurobourses part ways with U.S., Germany best bet.

text.p: Fresh from setting a string of record highs, most European bourses are parting ways with a seemingly unstoppable Wall Street, but analysts say Frankfurt is likely to emerge a better bet than London, Paris or Milan.

After climbing 1.7 percent in the last 10 days to 2,772.34 points on Thursday, analysts were sure the German blue-chip DAX index has the power to hit the 3,000 level in the next months and significantly outpace other European bourses in 1997.
While Wall Street's unbridled energy is often credited with hoisting Europe higher too, analysts said Germany, in particular, generates a separate upward momentum.

"Of course records on Wall Street create a good environment for all markets, but Germany enjoys its own dynamic which does not merely follow the U.S. market," said Hans-Peter Wodniok, head of German research at Credit Lyonnais in Frankfurt.
Key plus points for the German market are more favourable exchange rates fuelling the export oriented economy and an economic recovery showing ever more signs of picking up speed.

"The judgement is to start with economic recovery rather than the markets and the recovery favours moving into Germany and away from France, Italy, and the U.K.," said Peter Sullivan, equities strategist at Goldman Sachs in London.

Goldman Sachs forecast the DAX will climb 15 percent in the next twelve months, while the French CAC 40 index is seen rising only eight percent and the FTSE 100 of leading U.K. shares is expected to be flat to slightly lower.

For the German market, analysts agree, there is a much stronger correlation between what the dollar is doing than what Wall Street is doing. "If the dollar climbs, that will help us far more than if Wall Street climbs," Wodniok said, adding exchange rates could also unravel German gains.

German companies, including car-maker Daimler-Benz and chemicals and drugs giant Bayer AG, suffered lat year under the strong mark as exports were more expensive. Now they are enjoying higher foreign sales.
"As long as the dollar is trading above 1.50 marks, German companies will do fine," said one dealer.

At the same time investors are also enchanted with German industry's new-found commitment to the concept of share-holder value, promising leaner management structures and higher profit margins, all to deliver more value to shareholders.
"The market is giving German chief executives brownie points for boosting shareholder value and so long as they are credible, the shares will keep going higher," Wodniok added.
Just as Germany benefits from the weaker mark, Britain is struggling with firmer sterling as well as worries about rising interest rates.

Currently Britain is the only nation in Europe to face rising interest rates, "the fear of climbing rates is braking the bourse's move forward just as Sterling's appreciation is hurting with exports," said Franz Zendath, senior European equities analyst at Vereinsbank Research in Munich.

In Italy, analysts said a rigorous fiscal austerity programme, launched to prepare the nation to join Europe's planned currency union in 1999, may be the root of slower share market growth. Similarly important is the level at which the Italian lira will rejoin the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) as this will have an impact on exports.
"If Italy follows its plans these could weaken economic growth which would impact the bourse," Goldman's Sullivan said.

France, whose CAC-40 rose one percent in the last 10 days, may be seen to be in the middle, benefiting from economic recovery but still struggling with issues like pressing through savings packages to join the currency union.

As bourses dance ever higher, analysts are expecting a consolidation at some point. Hefty losses in New York would definitely affect European bourses, worsening sentiment, but in the longer run, dealers said a set-back could be used to buy again.
